name: Ironized Yeast

lead: Ironized Yeast was a tablet sold in the 1930s and later, promoted as a way for underweight people to gain weight and look fuller. Ads, often aimed at women, pitched it as a route to a more attractive figure and more energy.
It is a historical curiosity in weight-gain marketing. Yeast had been sold as a health product since the early 1900s, and the Federal Trade Commission questioned yeast advertising in the 1930s.

paras: It was sold as tablets taken as a supplement; the idea was that B vitamins from yeast and added iron would raise appetite and help weight gain.
No modern safety data on the original product were found. Iron supplements in general carry label cautions, and regulators in the 1930s questioned the advertising claims for yeast products.

angle.text: The product was marketed as a way for underweight people to add weight and a more filled-out look. The mechanism claimed was B vitamins and iron stimulating appetite.

lead: Ironized Yeast was a yeast-and-iron tablet advertised in the 1930s and after as a weight-gain aid for thin people, mostly women. Ads promised a fuller figure and appetite through B vitamins from yeast [1][2].

Dates vary across sources: a 1935 Motion Picture Magazine ad is documented, a 1933 print ad exists, and some accounts place later ads in the late 1940s [1]. Yeast products had been sold as health foods since the early 1900s, with Fleischmann's marketing yeast for complexion and digestion in the 1920s [3]. In the 1930s the FTC questioned yeast advertising, including doctors in ads and vague terms like internal fatigue [3].
No clinical studies of the product were found.

paras: Ads combined weight-gain claims with social messaging, one showing a woman who said men ignored her when thin and noticed her after gaining ten pounds [1]. Library Partners Press describes the company pitching a fuller figure and bigger appetite through B vitamin intake [2].

Fleischmann's Yeast for Health campaign reportedly raised yeast sales dramatically; later the FTC asked why the doctors shown in ads did not practice in America, and Fleischmann's agreed to run more careful advertising [3].

timeline.event: Fleischmann's promotes yeast as a health food [3]
